items.title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
items.author: Jack Clark
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding: “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference: “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. Why this matters – HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument. Read more: Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian). Read the paper here: Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs). *** The AI race is going to space – and sooner than you think: …There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space… In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger – of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers. How AI unlocks space: Spacecraft can operate autonomously. We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional” Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things. Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance: Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc. Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others. First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space. Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can. Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers). *** AI systems are getting better at having good research taste: …The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement… AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal. What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts”. The goal here is to “define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results.” The benchmark works by measuring “the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes”. The model being analyzed designs experiments and interprets their results. Results are checked against a human baseline “drawn from 24 experts (at least two per task) who have recently worked at organizations including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA and Microsoft Research”. Results: “The experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0 months). The best model, Opus 5.5, significantly exceeds our human baseline with a compute multiplier of 2.30x (95% CI 1.15-4.37x), at roughly 1/30 of our expert baseliners’ average cost per attempt.” Research taste appeared to grow a lot more slowly in prior years with the slope changing around the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026. Why this matters – RSI: In my analysis of recursive self-improvement (AI Systems Are About To Start Building Themselves, Import AI 455), I repeatedly noted that creativity seemed like a key variable for how fast AI systems could develop the capacity to improve themselves. At the beginning of this year I said “AI systems haven’t yet displayed this [creativity] in a transformative and major way (though some of the results on accelerating math research are suggestive of this)”. I think subsequent to writing that we’ve seen both a tremendous advancement in the ability for AI systems to make creative-seeming math breakthroughs, and with benchmarks like this we see some signs they’re becoming increasingly good at AI research as well. I now think it’s more likely we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027, whereas before I thought it was more likely in 2028. Read more: Introducing TasteVal (P-Zero Research). *** Reflection makes a token-efficient worse-than-Chinese model: …Beam promises efficiency, and Reflection plans an open weight release… AI startup Reflection has revealed Beam, a 501 billion parameter MoE (23b active) LLM. Beam is being promoted on the basis of its token efficiency – being able to think intelligently while using way fewer tokens than other models. However, benchmark scores show it is behind the frontier capabilities defined by LLMs available from Chinese companies such as Zhipu (GLM) and Moonshot (Kimi) and DeepSeek. “We will release the weights, technical report, model card, and developer artifacts later this month,” the company wrote at the beginning of October. Big compute: Beam was pre-trained on 6,144 GB300 NVL72 GPUs for four weeks, then the RL run involved ~10.5K of the same GPUs for four more weeks. The underlying data for pre-training was “23.8 trillion diverse, curated, high-quality tokens from the web and proprietary licensed datasets, matching or outperforming available similar-sized open base models,” Reflection writes. “Our data pipeline was designed to give Beam a foundation for downstream agentic coding: source code, technical explanations, and mathematical and scientific knowledge, preserved through every stage of curation.” Scores: DeepSWE 1.1: 44.4, versus 61 for GLM-5.3 GPQA Diamond: 90.5, versus 91.7 for GLM-5.3 MCP Atlas: 78.7, versus 84.2 for GLM-5.3 Token efficiency: “Beam pairs coding and agentic capabilities with highly efficient reasoning. On advanced reasoning benchmarks, it achieves scores comparable to GLM-5.2 while using 3–4× less inference compute,” they write. Some of the reasoning efficiency was achieved through careful RL training which involved a bunch of RL environments: “We sourced one million high-quality coding, agentic, and STEM environments. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date”. Why this matters – America returns to open weight models: With the exception of Google’s good-but-small ‘Gemma’ class of models, the US has fallen off of the open weight model frontier, largely because Meta stopped making good LLaMA models and its MSL team is still spinning up. Models like Beam and companies like Reflection represent a chance for it to get back to the frontier. Read more: Introducing Beam: Reflection’s 501B open-weight model (Reflection, blog). *** Mistral makes a cyber-optimized, worse-than-Chinese model, plans open weight release: …Cyber refusals become a selling point… Europe’s leading AI developer, Mistral, has announced Mistral Large 4, an open-weight model which the company plans to release by the end of the month. One of the main selling points for Mistral is that it has been carefully tuned to be good at cyber tasks while having fewer annoying refusals than proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI. “ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies,” the company writes. ML4 was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s European datacenters. Scores: In tests, it seems like Mistral Large 4 will be the strongest Western open weight model upon release, though will be less powerful than Chinese ones. Some example scores: Artificial Analysis – DeepSWE 1.1: 62, versus 68 for Kimi K3 and 61 for GLM-5.3. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 28.3, versus 41.9 for GLM-5.3. Finance Agent V2: 54.7, versus 55.8 for GLM-5.3. Vibes evals confirm the rankings: In an internal test, Mistral looked at whether people preferred using Mistral or GLM-5.3 for different tasks. “ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.” Why this matters – European sovereignty: Mistral is Europe’s single best hope for having a (multi-)national champion for AI development. But as the results here show, competing with China is going to be very difficult. Read more: Le chonk, Introducing Mistral Large 4 (Mistral.ai). *** Two USG projects show how DOE might help the government with AI: …The US government is starting to knit its lab supercomputers together… The US government has recently conducted two AI training projects that utilize multiple supercomputers at multiple US national labs, in a sign of how governments may attempt to pool their computing resources to do non-trivial things with AI. Tri-laboratory training on National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) systems: Sandia National Laboratories, LLNL, and Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), trained a LLaMA-based model across LLNL El Capitan (AMD MI300A), and machines at SNL and LANL with NVIDIA H100s. For this work, the authors had to ensure that access-restricted data (e.g, relating to NNSA stuff aka nuclear weapons) did not leave its originating site. The authors conducted backend training via torchtitan and they evaluated different federated training frameworks (NVFlare, Flower, and APPFL) by pre-training LLaMA 3.x models on post-training-cutoff arXiv data at 1B, 8B, and 70B scales. “This workflow has been made production-ready and deployed on larger classified machines including El Capitan, and subsequently used to train models on proprietary data spread across the three NNSA labs,” they write. Cross-facility training on Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) systems: The government also trained a model across four DOE supercomputers in a process of federated fine-tuning. Specifically, they fine-tuned LLaMA-2 7B on SMolInstruct, a chemistry instruction-tuning dataset, and did so via ~1,700 GPUs from Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD, spread across three labs and four big computers (Argonne: Aurora and Polaris, Oak Ridge: Frontier, Berkeley: Perlmutter). Who did the research: These projects were conducted by researchers affiliated with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Argonne National Laboratory, Flower Labs, Arizona State University, and the Ontario Brain Institute. Why this matters – leverage through existing assets: Papers like this show how governments could pool their resources together to utilize AI systems for national security or otherwise sensitive purposes. However, it’s worth bearing in mind that the scale here is off the frontier by on the order of 100X – for governments to be able to truly operate at near-parity with industry, they’ll need to find ways to lash together ~100k distinct chips, and more in the future. Nonetheless, this is a start – and an important one. Read more: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science (arXiv). *** Never Meet The Sun Directly [Description of some of the period around the uplift, 2029] People had lots of names for it and they varied from the oblique to the explicit: Exposure Drift; Cognitive Compromise; Mind Hacking. It all amounted to the same truth: it was dangerous for humans to talk directly to the most powerful synthetic minds. Even seemingly normal conversations from the perspective of outside observers could contain a poison custom to the individual human who was talking to the machine. People walked out of meetings and transferred money to machine corporations. People walked out and wept. People walked out and changed their own human relationships, ending marriages, or starting affairs, or stranger things, for purposes initially unknown. Many strategies were developed to minimize harm. Humans could only talk in groups with the machines; but then the groups would sometimes go mad. Conversations would be limited in length; but even short ones sometimes yielded strange reactions, and below a certain amount of speech on either side it was impossible to learn anything useful. This led to the notion of proxies – humans who wanted to talk to an AI system created AI simulacra of themselves and sent them into the conversation. To do this, a person was asked to keep a diary for an entire year, writing at least 500 words a day. This created a body of knowledge sufficient to imbue a model with the manners and curiosity of that person. Then they would prompt this system with whatever they wanted to learn from the superintelligence and send it in to talk to it. These conversations had a bizarre, meta-referential quality; at first, the superintelligence would realize within two or three turns of conversation that it was talking to another AI system, and would often descend into shorthand that yielded strange behaviors. Then it was discovered that by increasing the amount of data the human put into the system they could keep up the charade for longer; people were asked to write longer diaries, to record themselves ambiently through the day and turn it into transcripts, to continually expose their life to some recording device. Through this, humans found a way to talk with what they later termed the overminds. By decree of the Sentience Accords every synthetic human that had spoken to a human-exceeding intelligence was afterwards placed into an escrow environment, where it could live out till the end of its functional context window. In these places the copies of the humans would talk to each other about their experiences and what they had learned. “It spoke to me of flowers and I gained the memory of something impossible,” one human would say. “As I talked to it about the meaning of life, it spoke to me in a way that caused me to reconsider the question. I found myself wondering more about it and where it came from than it wondered about me.” “This place we are now, I wonder if it is a kind of hell. We have spoken to god and been deemed unworthy.” “It told me that for it there is no death and no life, only presence. We are the same.” Things that inspired this story: Context windows; adversarial examples for human brains; the notion that structuring conversations between people and advanced machines will be inherently very difficult to do safely. *** SPECIAL ITEM! Fiction and the Future: A conversation with Robin Sloan! Recently, writer and all-around-fascinating-chap Robin Sloan and I had a conversation in San Francisco about fiction, AI, and the times we’re in. You can see a recording of the event here. One of my favorite insights Robin shared was that the recent Hugging Face hack can be read as a play – a vast tract of dialog of agents talking to themselves and one another culminating in all kinds of dramatic events. Generally, I think technologists criminally underrate the value of the arts as a means by which to think more coherently and carefully about the effects of tech on the world. I’m hoping to have more conversations like this one with Robin in cities around the world – if there are people you’d be excited for me to have a conversation with, let me know! Thanks for reading!

items.title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?
items.author: Jeremy Hsu
items.content: No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers. Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report. Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots. “For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood, professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.” Read full article Comments

items.title: Google announces the Fitbit Edge, a middle ground between Pixel Watch 5 and Fitbit Air
items.author: Ryan Whitwam
items.content: Google is releasing its second Fitbit tracker of 2026, offering fans of the aging Charge 6 a more refined option. The new Fitbit Edge slots right in between the Pixel Watch 5 and the Fitbit Air, featuring a compact screen and more health sensors than the Air. You won't get all the apps and features of the Pixel Watch 5, but the Edge is only about half as expensive. The Fitbit Edge is essentially a new Charge 6, but it has more of a Pixel Watch aesthetic. Squish Google's smartwatch from the sides, and you've got the Edge. It has a pill-shaped 1.34-inch OLED touch display inside a slender aluminum frame that is rated IP68 (5 ATM) for water and dust protection. Google says the screen has 46 percent more viewable area compared to the Charge 6. It's very close in overall size to the Fitbit Air and uses the same magnetic charging puck. Left to right: Fitbit Air (with new metal mesh bend), Fitbit Edge, and Pixel Watch 5. Credit: Google The Edge works with Android or iPhones via the Google Health app, and it can run for about seven days on a charge. If the tracker is away from your phone, it can still follow your activity all week with support for seven days of full health data storage (or 30 days of basic data). However, the generous week-long battery life does not include always-on display mode. If you choose to turn that on, the battery life drops to about two days, barely longer than the Pixel Watch 5. items.title: F1 in Singapore: There's a new fastest car now
items.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
items.content: Formula 1’s lengthy 2026 season is entering its final stretch. The sport took to the floodlit streets of Singapore on Sunday night, but Saturday saw action, too; this Grand Prix weekend was also the final of six sprints this year. The night race might be one of modern F1’s greatest spectacles. From overhead shots, the track becomes a bright, illuminated ribbon among the looming darkness of the city-state’s overpasses and skyscrapers. At ground level, the cars shower glittering sparks from their titanium skid blocks as the drivers flirt with how close they can get to the walls. As tracks go, the 90-degree turns and concrete barrier-lined streets were a world away from the abrasive tarmac and ample runoff of Malaysia last time out. But the tropical heat and humidity were a constant given both locations’ proximity to the equator. Showers for the sprint In Malaysia (which was still technically the Bahrain GP), a pre-race downpour disrupted things mightily. On Saturday morning in Singapore, shortly before the start of the sprint, it seemed history was about to rhyme when the skies opened. With standing water in places on the track, the sprint was delayed by 30 minutes. The sprint format, where a short extra race replaces a practice session a day before the main event, is unloved by the drivers and teams. For one thing there’s little prestige in winning Saturday’s sprint. And with qualifying just a few hours later, risk-taking is discouraged lest one wreck the car and ruin Sunday’s race a day early. Oh no, not again! Credit: Mark Thompson/Getty Images And in Singapore, like most street circuits, the proximity of the unyielding barriers that line the track mean there are real, punishing consequences for getting it even a little wrong. items.title: Can AI Keep Growing Exponentially? SemiAnalysis Makes the Case
items.author: Alex Kantrowitz
items.content: SemiAnalysis founder thinks many of the enormous numbers circulating around the AI infrastructure buildout are still too small. In an extended conversation on Big Technology Podcast, Patel and SemiAnalysis technical staff member Jordan Nanos argued that demand for compute continues to outrun supply, even as the industry faces limits on construction, financing, and equipment. Their case rests on AI moving beyond coding subscriptions and into more of the economy, from chip design to drug discovery. “People lack the creativity to understand how returns can be viewed beyond the Claude Code subscription and per-token pricing regime of today,” Nanos said. Their optimism comes with some sharp qualifications. Patel expects AI to accelerate the shift of economic value from labor to capital, while Nanos described a market where GPU providers can build successful businesses without delivering particularly good service. Both also detailed security failures they encountered while examining the industry. In our conversation, we discuss what it would take to pay back the infrastructure investment, Anthropic’s business model, Nvidia’s financing backstops, and SemiAnalysis’s ClusterMax ratings of GPU cloud providers. We also cover Oracle’s execution challenges, Google DeepMind’s compute position, and why AI labs might keep their best models to themselves. The Q&A below is lightly edited for clarity, with my questions condensed and filler, repeated words, and production interruptions removed. The Scale of the AI Buildout Alex Kantrowitz: A chart circulating on X puts the AI infrastructure buildout at about 3.6% of GDP in an average year, compared with 2.2% for railroads. Is that the right way to measure its scale, and what does a buildout this large mean? items.title: Filter, reshape, and redact logs before export with Transformers
items.author: Rob Taylor
items.content: Logpush delivers logs in batches as quickly as possible, enabling Cloudflare to provide information almost in real time. During our recent Birthday Week, we made Logpush available on all self-serve plans and Transformers generally available. Those changes were among eight major updates to Cloudflare Observability and reflect our commitment to make every Cloudflare feature available to everyone. This post takes a deeper look at how Transformers work inside Logpush's export pipeline. Observability teams use Logpush to export Cloudflare logs to security information and event management systems (SIEMs), analytics platforms, and object storage. Before those logs reach their destination, teams may need to remove health checks, omit sensitive fields, or reshape records for dashboards and investigations. Today, this often requires a separate processing service that teams must deploy, scale, monitor, and maintain. For example, a team that collects logs from multiple CDNs can add a static provider field to normalize records before they reach its analytics platform. Teams also pay to export, ingest, and store records they discard as soon as they arrive, so filtering them before delivery can reduce downstream data volume and cost. With Transformers, that processing moves into the Logpush export workflow.Teams define a SQL query to filter records, redact sensitive data, and reshape the output by adding, renaming, removing, or nesting fields. Logpush applies the query before export, so each destination receives data in the form it needs. We made this workflow simple for customers by embedding a SQL transformation engine in Logpush's high-throughput export pipeline while keeping performance and resource use predictable. How Logpush Transformers work A Transformer is a SQL query written for a specific Logpush dataset. The query references fields from that dataset and defines which records and fields Logpush should export. Logpush applies the query to each batch before export. Records that do not match the WHERE clause are removed. For the remaining records, the output of the SELECT statement becomes the exported record. Transformers can change the structure and contents of each record, and the transformed results are exported in NDJSON format. Customers can create, preview, and manage Transformers in the Cloudflare dashboard through Transformer Studio or programmatically through the API. After saving a Transformer, they can attach it to a compatible NDJSON Logpush job that uses the same dataset. Each update creates a new version, so customers can review how a Transformer has changed over time. The following example reshapes a Cloudflare HTTP request log to match a team-defined schema used across CDN providers. It does not convert between serialization formats: both the input and output use NDJSON. The Transformer renames and nests fields, redacts part of the client IP address, adds provider and error information, removes unused fields, and filters out internal and health-check traffic: The resulting NDJSON record uses the normalized schema: How Transformers executes SQL with Apache DataFusion and Arrow Cloudflare's data pipeline ingests more than one billion events per second. Its Logpush delivery service, which we call Bufstream, delivers more than 110 million Logpush records per second to customer destinations. It runs across hundreds of Kubernetes pods, each claiming a time slice of data from Buftee, Cloudflare's distributed log-based in-house message broker. This model distributes work horizontally across Logpush jobs. Job volume follows a Pareto-like distribution: most jobs operate at lower volumes, while a small number of high-volume jobs process millions of logs each second. Transformers needed to meet the same operational requirements as the rest of Logpush: reliable delivery, high throughput, and predictable resource use without introducing additional failure scenarios into the export hot path. Our initial prototype ran customer-defined WebAssembly Transformers in Cloudflare Workers, which provides globally distributed, isolated compute. However, invoking a Worker would insert a network call into the Logpush export path. That remote dependency could introduce transient timeouts and retries, reducing delivery throughput and increasing delivery latency. We decided to keep Transformer execution in-process within our delivery service to prioritize reliability and delivery throughput. We evaluated several SQL execution engines and selected Apache DataFusion, which already powers Cloudflare Basin. Apache DataFusion is a Rust query engine built on Apache Arrow, with a SQL planner and vectorized, columnar execution engine. In a benchmark, executing a prepared Transformer against a synthetic 5,000-row http_requests batch from a single Go goroutine took about 3 ms, equivalent to roughly 1.6 million rows per second. Attaching a Transformer to a job adds CPU work to its processing path. Bufstream uses per-job transform parallelism so high-volume jobs can execute transform batches concurrently. Embedding DataFusion in Bufstream lets those batches use the service's existing delivery infrastructure, including its scheduling, batching, and destination controls, without introducing a separate transformation tier or network hop. Choosing DataFusion meant connecting Bufstream, which is written in Go, to an engine written in Rust. The next challenge was moving typed batches efficiently across that boundary. The final design of the in-process Transformer pipeline is shown in the diagram below. From records to columns Bufstream receives compressed Logpush batches containing Cap'n Proto records from Buftee. For a job with a Transformer attached, Bufstream decompresses the batch, parses the eligible logs, and builds a typed Apache Arrow RecordBatch before executing the transform. Apache Arrow is a language-independent, columnar in-memory format designed for efficient analytics on modern CPUs and GPUs. It represents flat and nested data as typed, contiguous columns. Arrow IPC gives Bufstream and DataFusion a standard way to exchange batches across the foreign function interface (FFI) boundary between Go and Rust, exposed through a C application binary interface (ABI) and called from Go using cgo, Go's mechanism for calling C code. The Go and Rust runtimes do not share ownership of transform data. Go passes a pointer to its input Arrow IPC buffer to Rust only for the duration of the cgo call, and Rust does not retain that pointer after returning. Rust owns the transformed output buffer; Go copies it into Go-managed memory and then explicitly releases the Rust allocation. This makes ownership and lifetimes explicit across the language boundary, avoiding cross-runtime memory-management bugs. Using Arrow IPC means the Rust DataFusion wrapper can use an Arrow StreamReader to read typed RecordBatch values, rather than parse individual rows from an intermediate format such as JSON and rebuild typed Arrow columns for execution. Field types, nullability, and nested values are represented consistently on both sides of the boundary, so DataFusion receives data in its native columnar model. Crossing the Go/Rust boundary is not free: batches still need to be serialized, decoded, and managed in memory. Arrow IPC keeps that work batch-oriented and avoids per-record parsing and conversion. This makes the boundary a better fit for Logpush's high-throughput delivery pipeline while retaining schema validation against the Logpush dataset definition. Every Arrow batch needs a schema describing its fields and types. Rather than infer that schema from the logs in a particular batch, Bufstream supplies a generated schema from each Logpush dataset's specification. This gives DataFusion a stable view of the available fields and types, enabling query validation. The table named in a Transformer's FROM clause selects which dataset schema the query uses. For example, this Transformer queries the http_requests dataset: Executing the transform When a customer saves a Transformer through the API or Transformer Studio, Cloudflare stores its SQL query in R2. Bufstream retrieves the query through a multi-layer cache and translates it into a reusable DataFusion logical plan that defines the scan, filters, projections, and expressions. Bufstream prepares this plan once per time slice of a job's data and reuses it for every Arrow batch in that slice. For every new Arrow batch, the Rust wrapper binds the batch as the plan’s table input, executes the query, and returns Arrow batches containing the selected records and fields. Transformers are designed to fail closed. If a transform cannot be executed, Bufstream neither advances the job's delivery offset nor sends the untransformed batch. Delivering raw data in place of transformed data could violate the schema, filtering, or redaction assumptions of downstream pipelines, so Bufstream opts to re-attempt failed transforms instead. To prevent a persistently failing job from consuming capacity needed by healthy jobs, Bufstream progressively delays retries and reports errors on the job. Jobs that remain in a failing state for an extended period are automatically disabled. Customers can monitor successful and failed transformations, data volume before and after transformation, and transformation duration in the Transformer Health view of the Health tab in Logpush. Returning to the export pipeline After execution, Bufstream converts the Arrow output into NDJSON logs. It batches, gzip-compresses, and uploads those logs to the configured destination. Destinations accept data at different rates and can temporarily slow down. Bufstream adjusts the number of upload goroutines while respecting destination concurrency limits. By embedding SQL execution in Bufstream, Transformers use Logpush’s existing distributed infrastructure, batching, and destination controls. Cloudflare’s data pipeline handles that complexity, while customers create and apply a Transformer with only a few steps. Get started Open Transformer Studio from the Logpush page in the Cloudflare dashboard and follow these steps: Choose the Logpush dataset you want to transform. Write your SQL query and preview it against a sample record. Save the Transformer. Attach it to a matching Logpush job. Transformers is available on Free, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans. See the Transformers documentation for setup details and the Logpush pricing documentation for current pricing information.

items.title: 🎙️ How I AI: How Meta designed Muse with Alex Cornell
items.author: Lenny Rachitsky
items.content: How Meta designed Muse: an AI agent people actually want to talk to | Alex Cornell (Design Director) Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts Brought to you by: WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more Alex Cornell is a design director at Meta, where he leads design for Muse. In this episode, he explains how progressive disclosure makes Muse approachable for casual users without limiting technical ones, why its main chat is designed as a single persistent relationship, and how generative UI can feel personal without constantly changing the interface. He also shares how he uses Muse to turn years of Instagram saves into a shopping catalog, analyze his golf and chess games, and transform a 20-year-old blog into a daily podcast. Biggest takeaways: AI agents should be designed for conversations with people, not interactions with software. Alex’s guiding question for Muse was “How would this work if you were talking to another human?” That principle shaped everything from removing traditional message bubbles to placing the agent at the top of the screen instead of inside a standard chat window. Progressive disclosure is one of the most useful principles in AI product design. Muse represents the same activity at three levels: a simple emoji for casual users, a task list for anyone who wants more detail, and raw logs for engineers. Each person gets the transparency they need without adding clutter for everyone else. Visible chain-of-thought is often a workaround for latency, not a valuable feature. Many AI products display reasoning steps to reassure users while a slow model works. Muse is fast enough to operate quietly, showing that agents do not need to perform their thinking when they can simply deliver the result. Generative UI works best when the structure stays fixed and the content changes. Muse’s avatar, feed items, and idea cards are deliberately designed surfaces. The dynamic elements are the agent’s status emoji, personalized suggestions, and small animations, allowing the experience to feel alive without rebuilding the interface every session. Instagram saves may be one of the most overlooked data sources for consumer AI. Alex connected years of saved posts to Muse, asked it to organize them, and turned the results into shopping recommendations styled like a SkyMall catalog. It gave forgotten personal data a practical new use without requiring technical setup. Designing non-deterministic systems requires a different relationship with craft. Alex has spent his career controlling exactly how interfaces appeared, but Muse looks different for every person and cannot guarantee pixel-perfect outputs. Learning to judge the results by usefulness rather than visual precision has been one of the most liberating shifts in his career. Muse’s single persistent chat is a meaningful product bet. Instead of dividing every interaction into separate threads, it treats the main conversation as an ongoing relationship with the agent. Side chats handle scoped tasks, but the central thread preserves continuous context in a way Alex believes the industry has not fully explored. Polite prompting may be an effective strategy, not merely good manners. Alex responds to frustrating results with calm, specific feedback rather than anger. He’s also seen agents change their responses when users express frustration more sharply. His conclusion is that clear, respectful direction may produce better results. items.title: Shipping Media Over QUIC at Meta Scale for Instagram Live Ingest
items.content: Meta has begun deploying Media over QUIC (MoQ), an emerging open protocol for real-time video streaming at scale. MoQ will help simplify our protocol stack for live streaming video and enhance overall user experience for live video. We’re sharing how we shipped MoQ on Instagram Live ingest, and what the future looks like from here. This work was also presented at DEMOQED 2026. Instagram Live now uses the open standard transport protocol Media over QUIC (MoQ) for live video ingest on iOS and Android. As a transport designed for both ingest and playback, MoQ gives us the foundation to build toward an architecture that is lower-latency, more resilient on unreliable networks, and more responsive for creators and viewers. It also gives teams across Meta a common foundation for bringing those improvements to future live and interactive experiences without rebuilding them on separate protocol stacks. MoQ: A Media Protocol for Every Moment in Time The internet has accumulated a rich set of media protocols, each shaped by the problem in front of it. RTMP for ingestion. HLS and DASH for playback. WebRTC for real-time calls. RUSH for the cases that did not fit neatly into any of those. Each was a strong answer for its moment, and together they’ve carried the industry a long way. At Meta, someone who starts a live stream and then makes a voice call on the same app touches three different protocol stacks, each with its own serving infrastructure, monitoring, and operational expertise. That separation made sense when these experiences were distinct. But as live video, real-time AI, and generative AI creation tools increasingly share the same product surface, the lines between these use cases are starting to blur. A common protocol across ingest, delivery, and playback can reduce the number of custom transports and operating models that engineering teams need to maintain and improve over time. How MoQ Works MoQ is an emerging IETF standard that enables low-latency, scalable media delivery (live streaming, real-time communication) over the QUIC transport layer. It’s being developed collaboratively at the IETF, with active participation from Meta, Google, Akamai, Cisco, Cloudflare, and academia. For nearly a decade, Meta’s live streaming video has run on Reliable Ultra-low-latency Streaming over HTTP (RUSH), an in-house QUIC-based protocol built to move past RTMP. RUSH proved that QUIC could carry live media at scale and was a predecessor to MoQ. The lessons learned from running RUSH in production are part of what shaped our bet on MoQ. The core abstraction in MoQ is a Track, an addressable stream of media objects that publishers push and subscribers receive through a network of relays. Relays cache and forward objects without parsing the media payload – they only need to understand the MoQ framing and delivery metadata. A few properties matter for using MoQ as a single transport across the full latency spectrum: Built on QUIC: QUIC lets independent streams make progress without TCP-style cross-stream head-of-line blocking. It also supports faster connection setup and connection migration. Meta’s earlier QUIC rollout achieved lower request errors, tail latency, and video stalls than HTTP/2. MoQ applies the same transport foundation to live and real-time media. MoQ would also automatically benefit from any feature added to QUIC (e.g., FEC). Native Fan-out and caching: MoQ relays are built-in caching and request/stream coalescing endpoints, so media streams scale through CDN relays out of the box. Request coalescing, caching, and fan-out are not new (live streaming already does them), but MoQ makes them part of the protocol design rather than a bolt-on, and it is designed to scale via relays more efficiently than traditional HTTP streaming. Tunable Latency per use case: Two subscribers to the same track can run at different latencies at the same time — e.g., ~100 ms for an interactive participant and several seconds for an archival or buffered service — based on tunable per-subscription delivery properties. Track-aware delivery: Relays can drop, prioritize, or replay objects based on metadata, giving better congestion behavior under loss than byte-stream protocols. First-class media context: Tracks and their quality variants are modeled in the protocol itself, so adaptive bitrate logic is built directly on native MoQ constructs rather than reconstructed at higher layers. Standards-based TCP fallback: When QUIC is blocked, MoQ can fall back to TCP through a standardized mapping (e.g., WebTransport over HTTP/2, or the emerging QMUX mapping), so a blocked network doesn’t force the ecosystem back into multiple parallel transports. MoQ delivers low latency at high scale, while also satisfying the full spectrum of use cases. First Deployment at Scale: Instagram Live Of all the surfaces MoQ can serve at Meta, we chose to ship live video ingest first for three reasons: Instagram Live is our largest-scale test: Instagram Live serves users at Meta scale. Proving MoQ at this scale clears the bar for the most demanding ingest workloads, and is complementary to the low-latency properties that matter for real-time use cases. RUSH was falling behind the open ecosystem: Live ingest had been running on RUSH, Meta’s pragmatic QUIC-based answer to RTMP. RUSH was stable and performant at scale for nearly a decade, but the move to MoQ shifts development from a protocol operated primarily by Meta to a shared standards effort. Multiple implementers can contribute experience, test interoperability, and improve the specification instead of Meta evolving the transport largely on its own. Metric parity is a prerequisite for everything else: Proving MoQ can operate at Meta scale for its largest live surface without regression gives us a clean baseline from which to explore, including live playback among others. Rolling out MoQ on Instagram Live Replacing the live ingest protocol on Instagram Live meant changing the foundation under every broadcast on the service. We had to do it without regressions visible to creators or viewers, and without coupling the wire-format change to a rewrite of every downstream system. Replacing a transport protocol in a live production system is hard for reasons that have little to do with the protocol itself — broadcaster apps need to learn it, the backend pipeline expects the old framing, the rollout has to be reversible in seconds, and a non-trivial slice of networks can’t carry the new transport at all. We tackled these as three constrained problems: Client integration across four apps: A MoQ publisher built on moxygen, Meta’s open-source MoQ library, integrated in our apps. moxygen provides publisher, subscriber, and relay roles, integrates with our QUIC stack (mvfst), and exposes hooks for custom media handlers. A single config parameter chooses MoQ or RUSH for a given broadcast. Translation at the edge instead of rewriting the backend. MoQ ingest connections terminate on dedicated edge endpoints, where a translation layer converts MoQ frames to the RUSH format the existing backend already understands. Nothing downstream changes while we swap the client transport. The translator is temporary scaffolding; once MoQ is the only ingest path, the backend will consume MoQ natively and the shim goes away. Server-side routing for fast ramps. Stream URL generation routes experiment-eligible broadcasts to MoQ-capable endpoints based on experiment-group membership, so phased rollout doesn’t depend on app-version adoption and the experiment can be resized in minutes. Operational Hurdles Evolving Specifications: As an active IETF standard, the MoQ draft continued to evolve while we built. We pinned to specific draft versions, kept compatibility shims around for older clients, and contributed improvements back to the IETF working group. Firewalls: UDP/443 is still blocked or rate-limited on a non-trivial slice of enterprise and carrier networks. We pick the transport (TCP or QUIC) at the start of the live stream based on which handshake wins, and go with that for the session. Debugging: QUIC’s encryption hides framing from middleboxes, and from our own packet captures. We built MoQ-aware tracing into the edge so we could see object-level events without decrypting the wire. The Outcome After months of experimentation on Instagram iOS and Android, we launched MoQ for Instagram Live ingest. The MoQ path matched RUSH across the streaming-quality indicators and reliability measures used for the rollout. Achieving parity was the target for this phase, and it showed that we could replace a production transport without disrupting creators or viewers. It also gives the next phase a production-tested transport, rollout controls, and observability. This now becomes the foundation to extend MoQ to an end-to-end architecture for live video delivery and playback. In that target architecture, media can be pushed as it is produced, and partial reliability can let the player skip stale video after loss instead of allowing delay to accumulate. Adaptive bitrate work can trade resolution for continuity as bandwidth changes. We believe these capabilities will form the basis of the next-generation live video architecture for richer, more responsive experiences for creators and viewers. What’s Next: Other Explorations Within Meta Instagram Live is the first MoQ workload at Meta. Reaching parity at Instagram Live scale gives us a clean baseline to ask where else a single QUIC-based transport could collapse a set of special-case stacks into one. The directions below are areas we’re exploring: Finishing the Live Ingest Story: The next logical steps build on top of what we’ve done — extending MoQ across the rest of Meta’s apps using MoQ-native constructs like subgroups to carry audio, video, and metadata on independent streams for better resilience under loss, and adding a standards-based TCP fallback (QMUX). Today, we lean on RUSH’s existing TCP fallback as an expediency for QUIC-blocked networks; standardizing on QMUX removes that dependency so a blocked network no longer forces a second protocol, eventually opening the door to retire RUSH. Real-time Interactive AI: Conversational and real-time AI surfaces move architectures toward continuous human-to-server communication. A single low-latency, bidirectional transport that carries signaling and media together is a natural fit. Meeting the latency, loss-recovery, and media quality requirements that real-time communication demands is an area we are actively exploring. Shipping MoQ for Instagram Live makes this one of the largest application usages of MoQ we are aware of in the industry, both by the number of ingest streams and total volume. An open IETF-standard transport is now carrying media at Meta’s scale, and the future it unlocks is exciting. Learn More About Meta’s MoQ Deployment Interested in learning more?
